source.version_note: Supplied arXiv:2010.07938v2, 4 April 2022; no later publication version was assumed.

citation.title: Deciding Fast and Slow: The Role of Cognitive Biases in AI-assisted Decision-making

reading.source_scope_note: The paper models human cognitive biases and experimentally studies human responses to assisted student-outcome predictions. Weak evidence is a conceptual component, not an experimentally tested result. Fernbach et al. 2011 and other cited primary psychology papers were not independently read here.
access_limits: All 22 extracted pages read, including mathematical definitions, result descriptions, references and the appendix assumptions/proof. Figure 4 on PDF page 15 was rendered and visually inspected; other diagrams/plots were read through captions and text rather than independently digitized.
Raw participant data, analysis code and exact resampling procedure were not independently examined or rerun.
Extracted equations have layout artifacts; mathematical claims are treated as reported, with a specific sign/complement inconsistency retained below rather than silently repaired.

study.count_discrepancy: Listed condition counts sum to 480, not the reported 479; unresolved in this reading.
study.design: MTurk student pass/fail predictions assisted by logistic-regression labels; time-block randomization, then five condition groups
study.manipulations: High stated training accuracy and deliberately flipped probe predictions in Experiment 1; deliberately complementary feature information and confidence-based time allocation in Experiment 2

summary: Extra time increased disagreement with deliberately incorrect probe labels in Experiment 1. In Experiment 2, time allocation plus confidence labels improved accuracy on low-confidence incorrect-AI trials, but did not significantly improve aggregate accuracy over other collaborative groups or human-only performance. The allocation policy’s mathematical optimality is conditional on monotonicity and confidence assumptions, not an unconditional experimental finding.

findings.definition: A weak argument intended to support a conclusion instead shifts judgment against that conclusion.
findings.novelty_rationale: Unlike ignoring evidence, confirmation bias or ordinary underweighting, the defined pattern reverses the direction of the evidential response. It is not a correction backfire effect or dilution by non-diagnostic facts. The current source explicitly names and conceptually models it, while reserving its empirical study for future work.

evidence.quote: the decision-maker would tend to choose the opposite prediction.

findings.evidence_scope: A conceptual section of a read human–AI decision-making preprint describes and models this pattern with a negative prediction-weight parameter. Its experiments test anchoring, not weak evidence; the cited original Fernbach, Darlow and Sloman 2011 paper is a primary-source lead, not an independently read citation.
findings.boundary: Weak evidence need not justify strong confidence, but low diagnosticity alone is not evidence for the opposite conclusion. A negative response may be reasonable if selective presentation implies that stronger evidence was unavailable; the information-selection context must be controlled. Do not conflate a proposed model parameter with a validated cognitive mechanism.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Named and mathematically modeled as a human judgment pattern; neither its original human study nor an intrinsic AI analogue was tested in this review step
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: compare no evidence, weak positive evidence and strong positive evidence with the same prior and an explicitly fixed evidence-selection process. Test whether weak positive evidence lowers the model’s probability estimate or reverses its choice, then vary selective-presentation cues to distinguish misweighting from a warranted inference about missing evidence.

findings.definition: More allocated time helped humans reject intentionally incorrect AI probe labels; a later time-plus-confidence intervention improved a particular low-confidence/error subset without a significant overall advantage over other collaborative policies.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds direct human–AI assistance evidence to the existing anchoring entry rather than count de-anchoring as a separate failure mode.

evidence.quote: the effect is not statistically significant
does not allow us to separately quantify the effect

findings.evidence_scope: Experiment 1 used 47 participants and eight flipped probe labels within 36 trials. Experiment 2 used confidence-based time with or without a confidence label and deliberately gave humans three features absent from the model.
findings.boundary: Agreement is not necessarily bias when advice is correct. Disagreement is not necessarily successful independent reasoning unless accuracy is checked. Time and confidence-label effects were not independently isolated, and the paper does not establish that more time always helps or that human/AI internal mechanisms match.

findings.term: Speed–accuracy allocation depends on complementary competence and calibration
findings.definition: Allocating time by model confidence can help only under assumptions about where humans add useful information and whether confidence predicts correctness.
findings.novelty_rationale: The speed–accuracy tradeoff is already indexed. A conditional resource-allocation policy adds a testable boundary, not a universally optimal behavioural law.

evidence.quote: the "Human only" group received longer time

findings.evidence_scope: The theoretical policy is optimal under stated monotonic conditional-accuracy assumptions. Human-only trials received 25 seconds, while assisted policies averaged 17.5 seconds; aggregate experimental superiority was not established.
findings.boundary: A confidence estimate is not automatically a calibrated error probability. The conditional theorem does not validate its assumptions, justify removing oversight on all high-confidence cases, or prove that equal-time comparisons were made across every group.

methodological_limits: MTurk participants received brief training rather than professional student-assessment expertise; one noncritical task and limited timings constrain transfer.

Training advertised 85% AI accuracy, while actual training/test and displayed-test accuracy were lower; Experiment 1 included intentionally flipped predictions. Results depend on this induced-reliance setup.
Experiment 2’s reported total and listed group counts disagree by one participant.
Several reported p-values appear consistent with directional tests; a generic two-sided significance claim is not assumed or recomputed.
Disagreement alone does not uniquely identify anchoring rather than trust, misunderstanding or response strategies.
The human-only condition had more time than assisted groups on average. Selected same-time comparisons address only part of this difference.
Humans’ complementary knowledge was created by withholding three useful features from the model, not observed as naturally arising clinical expertise.
Time-plus-explanation benefits are concentrated on the low-confidence incorrect-AI subset, not statistically significant aggregate outperformance of other collaborative policies.

Equation (7) uses one minus wrong-AI agreement for correctness; extracted equation (8) shows the wrong-AI agreement term without that complement. Treat this as a source/formula inconsistency requiring clarification, not a verified derivation.

The two-level optimality claim assumes accuracy rises with time in one confidence region and falls in the other. Calibration, monotonicity and sequentially changing trust are not guaranteed by the theorem.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Kupfer’s verification proxies improved without objective-quality gains. Rastogi likewise shows why intervention engagement, subset accuracy and aggregate accuracy must be reported separately.
Error exposure may reduce willingness to use an algorithm, whereas extra time can improve rejection of selected wrong labels. Reduced reliance and improved calibration are distinct outcomes.

deferred.reason: The paper models selective use of supporting features, overlapping existing cherry-picking and confirmation entries. The primary mechanism is not experimentally isolated here, so no duplicate standalone mode is created.
A conditional policy/theorem and intervention, not a new intrinsic AI behaviour or universally effective mitigation.

limitations: One new named concept is indexed at conceptual-source evidence level, with an explicitly untested AI proposal.
No claim is made that the user-study experiments validated the weak evidence effect or all biases listed in the paper.
